feedback.note: The sentence holds because life is action the organism generates in order to sustain itself. Stillness would turn life into a condition with no action, and a decree would place the goal outside the organism, which drops the self-generated character of living action.

exercises.prompt: What does a human being lack, even though his life requires him to deal with the world?

choices.text: An automatic code of knowledge and of values
A body that is able to act
Sensory organs that give him material for awareness
The alternative of continuing to live or of dying

feedback.note: Man has no automatic code of knowledge or of values, so he must discover what his life requires. He does have a body, senses, and the alternative of life or death. Treating those as the thing he lacks fails because they are part of his nature, not the missing code.

exercises.prompt: How does an animal stay within the range its kind of life requires?

choices.text: By forming concepts and judging long-range consequences
By automatic sensory guidance, including pleasure and pain
By having no goal, since only human beings act in order to live
By an innate set of philosophical principles it applies

feedback.note: An animal's goal-directed action is guided automatically by sensation, perception, and pleasure and pain, within the range its body is built for. Conceptual judgment is man's method, not the animal's. Denying animal goals fails because an animal's action is still aimed at its life.

exercises.prompt: A person strongly wants to stay alive. What does that desire fail to supply?

choices.text: Any evidence that he is a living organism
The possibility of choosing, which a desire cancels
Knowledge of how to live, and a code of values that selects the means
The fact that his life can succeed or fail

feedback.note: A desire to live is not knowledge of how to live. The wish shows that he wants the outcome, and it does not identify the actions that will secure it. Treating the desire as a cancellation of choice fails because the desire is not a code that takes the choosing out of his hands.

exercises.prompt: Match each kind of life to the guidance it actually has.

pairs.right: Automatic physical action suited to its life
Automatic sensory guidance within its range
No innate code of knowledge or of values
Not knowledge of the means of living

feedback.note: Plants and animals sustain themselves by automatic guidance suited to their kind, while a human being has no innate code of knowledge or of values. Equating a desire to live with that code fails because the desire does not identify the means. Man's lack is the code, not the fact of being alive.

exercises.prompt: Someone says man has an instinct of self-preservation that tells him what to do. Where is the error?

choices.text: He has no such instinct. Wanting to live does not identify the actions that will keep him alive
The error is wanting to live, which a rational being should not do
He has the instinct, and reason's job is to talk him out of survival
Instincts are concepts he composes at birth and then forgets

feedback.note: An instinct of self-preservation is what man does not possess. The desire to remain alive does not name which actions will sustain him, so it is not a code of knowledge or of values. Calling the wish itself the error fails because the wish is not the missing knowledge, and it is not a vice.

exercises.prompt: He is born with no innate knowledge of how to live. Which conclusion does that fail to justify?

choices.text: He must discover what his life requires
A desire to live is not yet a code of values
His conceptual faculty does not arrive already stocked with conclusions
He has no nature, and therefore his life has no requirements

feedback.note: No innate code means the content of knowledge and of values is not given. It does not mean he has no nature. Dropping his nature fails because he is a living organism of a specific kind, and that kind is what makes the requirements of his life real.

exercises.prompt: Complete the principle about what a desire to live does not supply.

parts.text: A desire to live is not

feedback.note: A desire to live is not knowledge of how to live, because wanting the result does not identify the means. Treating the desire as proof fails because a wish is not evidence about which actions sustain life, and a command or a vote fails because neither is the missing knowledge.

exercises.prompt: Build the principle that names what man lacks at the start.

feedback.note: Man has no innate code of knowledge or of values, so nothing in him already selects how to live. A finished instinct would restore the code he does not possess, and automatic certainty would pretend the conclusions are given. A desire to live still would not be that code.

exercises.prompt: Which faculty is man's means of survival in the world?

choices.text: Reason, the faculty that identifies and integrates what the senses provide
An instinct that already contains the knowledge his life requires
Faith that bypasses the evidence of the senses
A group's consensus, accepted in place of his own identification

feedback.note: Reason is man's means of survival because it identifies and integrates the material his senses provide, which is how he discovers what his life requires. Instinct fails because he has no such code, faith fails because it skips the evidence, and consensus fails because a group is not a faculty of knowledge.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about the faculty of reason?
exercises.quote: Reason is the faculty that identifies and integrates the material provided by man's senses.

choices.text: Reason identifies and integrates the material the senses provide
Reason creates the sensory material and then integrates what it created
The senses already deliver finished knowledge, so integration is optional
Reason is a feeling about sensory material, not a faculty of identification

feedback.quote: Reason is the faculty that identifies and integrates the material provided by man's senses.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "The Objectivist Ethics," The Virtue of Selfishness, 20
feedback.note: The passage establishes that reason identifies and integrates the material the senses provide, which is why reason can be a means of knowledge. Creation fails because the faculty does not invent its material, finished delivery fails because integration would then be unnecessary, and a feeling fails because reason is not an emotion about the senses.

exercises.prompt: A farmer identifies soil, rain, and seed, then integrates them into a plan that will feed him. Which faculty is doing that work?

choices.text: An instinct that already knew the harvest
Reason, working on the material his senses provide
A feeling that the crop will appear if he wants it strongly enough
Custom, followed without identifying what the field requires

feedback.note: The farmer's means is reason, because he identifies and integrates sensory facts into a plan his life depends on. Instinct fails because no innate code already knows the harvest, and feeling or custom fails because neither identifies what the field in fact requires.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to its role in the means by which a human being survives.

pairs.right: Provide the material to be identified
Identifies and integrates that material
Depends on the use of that faculty
A claimed means that skips the evidence

feedback.note: The senses provide material, and reason identifies and integrates it, which is why human survival depends on that faculty. Faith fails as a means because it claims knowledge while skipping the evidence reason would have to identify. Instinct is not a rival means he actually has.

exercises.prompt: Why can reason serve as the means of survival when no instinct supplies a code?

choices.text: Because it lets him ignore the facts and remain alive anyway
Because it runs by itself, as a plant's physical processes do
Because it can discover, from the facts, what his life requires and how to get it
Because survival does not require any knowledge of the world

feedback.note: Reason can be the means of survival because it is able to discover, from the facts, what his life requires. Ignoring the facts fails because unidentified requirements are not met by refusing to look, and an automatic run fails because reason is not a plant's chemistry. Survival does require knowledge.

exercises.prompt: He grants that reason integrates evidence, then adds a revelation for whatever reason has not finished. What is the error?

choices.text: He has no second means of knowledge. A revelation does not identify the facts
The error is using reason on evidence in the first place
The faster claim is the true one, so speed can replace identification
Two contradictory methods can both be means of knowledge if he prefers them

feedback.note: Revelation is not a means of knowledge, because it does not identify and integrate the facts his life depends on. A second method fails because a contradiction between methods is not two ways of knowing. Speed fails as a standard because a fast claim can still be false.

exercises.prompt: Complete the principle that names man's means of survival.

feedback.note: Man's means of survival is reason, the faculty that identifies and integrates what the senses provide. Instinct fails because he has no automatic code, faith fails because it skips evidence, and consensus fails because another person's agreement is not a substitute for identification.

exercises.prompt: Build the principle that says what reason does with the material of the senses.

feedback.note: Reason identifies and integrates the material the senses provide, which is why it can guide action. Saying reason creates that material fails because the faculty apprehends what is given, and saying it may ignore the material fails because there is then nothing left to identify.

exercises.prompt: Does the mere possession of reason guarantee that a person will think?

choices.text: No. The faculty works by his choice to focus his mind or not
Yes. Reason runs automatically, in the way digestion does
Yes. A group thinks for him whenever he possesses the faculty
No, because thinking is impossible and the faculty is a fiction

feedback.note: Reason does not run by itself. The choice to think is the choice to focus, so possession of the faculty is not its exercise. An automatic run fails because conceptual thought is volitional, and a group fails because no other mind can focus his. Skepticism fails because the choice is a real use of a real faculty.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about the choice to think?
exercises.quote: Psychologically, the choice "to think or not" is the choice "to focus or not."

choices.text: Thinking and focusing are separate faculties, and only focusing is a choice
The choice to think and the choice to focus are one and the same choice
Focusing is an emotion, and that emotion reports the facts directly
Chemistry performs the choice, so the person himself does not

feedback.quote: Psychologically, the choice "to think or not" is the choice "to focus or not."
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, "The Objectivist Ethics," The Virtue of Selfishness, 21
feedback.note: The passage establishes that the choice to think or not is the choice to focus or not, so putting reason to work is that one volitional act. Separate faculties fail because they would split a single choice. An emotion fails because it would make focus a feeling rather than the act of using one's mind, and chemistry fails because it would deny that the choice is his.

exercises.prompt: A person could learn that a bridge is unsafe, and he does not bother to look. What has he left unused?

choices.text: An instinct of self-preservation that should have decided for him
Reason. The means of survival does not inspect the bridge in his place
A body that knows the structure without any awareness of it
The facts, which become safe because he refused to look

feedback.note: He has left reason unused, because the faculty identifies the danger only if he chooses to look. An instinct fails as the substitute because he has none that labels the bridge, and the facts do not become safe because he blanked out. His means of survival does not act in his place.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to what it contributes to surviving by reason.

pairs.right: A capacity, not a guarantee that he thinks
The choice by which he uses that capacity
The choice not to think
Required if the thinking is to sustain his life

feedback.note: Having reason is only the capacity. Focusing is the choice to use it, drifting is the choice not to, and action is required because an unused conclusion does not sustain life. Treating possession as a guarantee fails because the faculty does not run by itself.

exercises.prompt: Reason has identified a real danger. What is still required if he is to survive by that knowledge?

choices.text: A stronger feeling, to replace the conclusion he has reached
A declaration that rewrites the danger out of existence
Action in line with what he knows. An unused conclusion does not sustain him
Nothing further, because knowing is the whole of survival

feedback.note: Surviving by reason takes the choice to think and the choice to act on what he knows. A feeling fails as a replacement because it does not change the danger, and a declaration fails because it does not rewrite the fact. Knowledge he will not act on leaves the requirement unmet.

exercises.prompt: He says he need not think, because other people are thinking and his life is therefore secure. What is left out?

choices.text: His life still depends on his own choice to judge his situation, including what others claim
Other people can never know a fact he has not discovered entirely alone
Their thinking changes the facts, so his own judgment would be a duplicate
Security is a feeling, and a feeling is a means of knowledge

feedback.note: Another person's thinking does not focus his mind. He can learn from others only by his own judgment of their claims and of his situation. Demanding that he discover every fact alone fails because learning is possible, and it is still his choice to think. Their thought does not rewrite the facts he must judge.

exercises.prompt: Complete the principle about the act by which reason is put to work.

parts.text: Reason is put to work by the choice to

feedback.note: Reason is put to work by the choice to focus, because the faculty does not run by itself. Drift fails because it is the choice not to think, and obeying or wishing fails because neither identifies the facts. Another person's thinking does not perform this act for him.

exercises.prompt: Build the principle that says when reason actually sustains life.

feedback.note: Reason sustains life only if one chooses to think and to act, because the faculty is volitional and a conclusion he will not enact leaves him where he was. Automatically would deny the choice, and without acting would treat unused knowledge as if it already sustained him.

exercises.prompt: What does this passage establish about man's nature?
exercises.quote: The key to what you so recklessly call "human nature," the open secret you live with, yet dread to name, is the fact that man is a being of volitional consciousness.

choices.text: Man's distinctive fact is that his consciousness operates by choice
Human nature is an innate code of knowledge he does not have to discover
Volition means his consciousness creates the facts it is aware of
Consciousness is an ornament added to an automatic animal code

feedback.quote: The key to what you so recklessly call "human nature," the open secret you live with, yet dread to name, is the fact that man is a being of volitional consciousness.
feedback.citation: Ayn Rand, Galt's Speech, For the New Intellectual, 120
feedback.note: The passage establishes that man is a being of volitional consciousness, so his distinctive fact is that his consciousness operates by choice. An innate code fails because nothing automatic supplies his knowledge, creating the facts fails because volition is not a power to rewrite reality, and an ornament fails because the volitional faculty is his means of dealing with the world.

exercises.prompt: Why is a rational animal one kind of organism, rather than two beings placed side by side?

choices.text: Animal names a machine, and rational names a ghost that lives in it
He is a living organism, and reason is his specific means of sustaining that life
Rational cancels the fact that he is alive and must act to remain so
Animal means he survives by instinct, and rational names an optional extra

feedback.note: Man is one living organism whose means of survival is reason, which is what the single designation rational animal names. A ghost in a machine fails because it splits him in two, and an optional extra fails because reason is the means, not a decoration on an instinct he does not have.

exercises.prompt: A theory calls man goal-directed, concludes that instinct already knows his good, and treats reason as a late ornament. What has it dropped?

choices.text: That he has no automatic code, and that reason is the means he must choose to use
That he is alive and that his actions can be aimed at his life
That plants survive by forming conceptual plans
Nothing. An ornament and a means of survival are the same fact

feedback.note: Goal-direction is true of him as a living organism, and it does not give him an instinct that knows his good. Dropping the missing code fails because a desire to live is not knowledge of how to live, and calling reason an ornament fails because that faculty is the means he must use.

exercises.prompt: Match each part of man's nature to the fact it names.

pairs.right: Goal-directed, self-sustaining action
Knowledge and values are not given automatically
The means of survival he must choose to use
Awareness that operates by choice

feedback.note: The four names are one picture: a living organism, no automatic code, and reason as the means that works only by choice. Volitional consciousness names that last fact. An instinct that already knows his good fails because it puts back the code the picture removes.

exercises.prompt: Which set of claims, taken together, is the rational animal?

choices.text: A living being whose instinct is the code, with reason as decoration
A mind that is not an organism and needs no self-sustaining action
An organism whose wishes set the facts, which reason then records
A living being with no automatic code, who survives by choosing to use reason

feedback.note: The rational animal is a living being with no automatic code, who survives by choosing to use reason. An instinctive code fails because he does not have one, a disembodied mind fails because he is an organism, and wishes fail because they do not set the facts reason has to identify.

exercises.prompt: A man is hungry, and he has no innate knowledge of which plants will nourish him. What does his nature require?

choices.text: That he eat whatever he feels like eating, because the desire is the knowledge
That the hunger proves reason is unnecessary for the problem of food
That he use reason to identify what will nourish him, and that he act on it
That he wait until an instinct labels the plants as safe or deadly

feedback.note: Hunger is a real fact of a living organism, and it is not knowledge of which plants are food. His nature requires him to identify the means by reason and to act, because he has no automatic code. Treating the desire or an instinct as the label fails because neither identifies the plants.

exercises.prompt: Complete the principle that names what a rational animal must do in order to live.

parts.text: A rational animal survives by choosing to use

feedback.note: A rational animal survives by choosing to use reason, because he is a living being with no innate code. Instinct fails because he has no automatic code of knowledge or of values, wishes fail because a desire to live is not knowledge of how to live, and consensus fails because a group is not his means of survival.

exercises.prompt: Build the principle that holds the rational animal in one statement.

feedback.note: A rational animal survives by choosing to use reason rather than an innate code, because he is a living being whose consciousness is volitional and whose life is not pre-programmed. Automatically would restore an instinct he does not have, and wishing would pretend the facts obey the desire to live.

exercises.prompt: What is a need of a living being, as against a wish?

choices.text: A requirement of its life, set by the kind of organism it is
Any strong wish, because intensity turns a preference into a requirement
A luxury it enjoys once its life is already secure
Whatever name other people assign, whether its life requires that thing or not

feedback.note: A need is a requirement of a living being's life, set by the kind of organism it is. Intensity fails because a strong wish need not be something the life depends on, a luxury fails because pleasure is not the test, and a name assigned by others fails because the requirement is a fact about the organism.

exercises.prompt: Food keeps an animal alive, and a particular ornament is only wanted. What is the difference?

choices.text: There is no difference, because both can be felt
Food is required by that life. The ornament is a preference the life does not require
The ornament is a need whenever the preference is strong
Food is a need only after a group declares it to be one

feedback.note: Food is a need because that kind of life depends on it, while the ornament is a preference the life does not require. Feeling both fails as a test because a wish is not a requirement. Strength fails for the same reason, and a group's declaration fails because the organism's nature, not a vote, sets the need.

exercises.prompt: A luxury can be a real pleasure and still fail to be a need. Why?

choices.text: Pleasure is what proves that something is a need
Anything that can be bought is a need
Pleasure is not the test. A need is set by what that kind of life depends on
Requirements of life are whatever happens to be scarce

feedback.note: A luxury can please and still not be a need, because a need is what that kind of life depends on, not what is delightful or for sale. Scarcity fails because a rare ornament is not thereby a requirement of life. Pleasure is real, and it is not the standard that distinguishes a need from an extra.

exercises.prompt: Match each term to its relation to a living organism.

pairs.right: Something that kind of life requires
A wish the life does not require
A pleasure that is not a requirement
The fact that makes a requirement real

feedback.note: A need is what that kind of life requires, a whim is a wish that is not required, and a luxury is a pleasure that is not a requirement. The organism's life is what makes the difference real, because only a living being can gain or lose by meeting or missing a requirement. A strong feeling does not redraw the line.

exercises.prompt: Someone says nothing is a need, because different people want different things. What is the error?

choices.text: Subjectivism. Wants vary, and the requirements of a living nature do not vanish with them
The error is admitting that organisms are alive
He is right, because a nature would have to be one person's wish
Needs are innate ideas, so the variation of wants is irrelevant for that other reason

feedback.note: The error is subjectivism about needs. Wants vary, and the requirements of a living nature do not become optional because they vary. Equating nature with a wish is the same error. Innate ideas are the wrong correction, because a need is a fact about the organism's life, not a conclusion written into the mind at birth.

exercises.prompt: Is a need the same thing as a value one has already achieved?

choices.text: Yes. What is still unmet is only a whim
Yes. Hunger, for example, is knowledge that one has already eaten
No. Needs do not exist until a law gives them a name
No. A need is a requirement, and it can be unmet. The name does not mean it has been satisfied

feedback.note: A need is a requirement, so it can be real while unmet. Calling the unmet a whim confuses a requirement with a satisfied value. Hunger is not knowledge that one has eaten. A law's name fails because the requirement is set by the organism, not by a statute. Naming the need does not by itself meet it.

exercises.prompt: Complete the principle that says what a need is a requirement of.

parts.text: A need is a requirement of an organism's

feedback.note: A need is a requirement of an organism's life, set by the kind of being it is. A whim fails because wanting is not depending, status fails because rank is not a biological or rational requirement, and a luxury fails because an extra pleasure is not what the life needs in order to go on.

exercises.prompt: Build the principle that distinguishes a need from a wish.

feedback.note: A need is what that kind of life requires, so the kind of organism sets it and a mere wish does not. A whim would make intensity the standard, and a luxury would make pleasure the standard. Neither is the dependence of a living being on what its nature requires.

exercises.prompt: Why do a fish and a man not share one list of needs?

choices.text: Needs follow from the kind of organism, and their natures differ
They do share one list, because every living thing is interchangeable
A committee assigns each list with no regard to either nature
Needs are whims, so the kind of organism does not matter

feedback.note: Needs follow from the kind of organism, so a fish and a man do not share one list. Interchangeability fails because their natures differ, a committee fails because it cannot rewrite those natures, and whims fail because a requirement is not a preference. The difference in needs is a difference in identity.

exercises.prompt: What sets a fish's need of water apart from the needs of a man?

choices.text: Whichever list happens to be longer
The kind of organism each is. One nature's requirement is not the other's
The element each of them happens to like more
A decree that is free to ignore both natures

feedback.note: The kind sets the needs, so water is a requirement of the fish's life and not a template for man's. Length, liking, and a decree fail because none of them is the organism's nature. Copying one list onto the other kind ignores the identity that makes a requirement a requirement.

exercises.prompt: What goes wrong if a man is assigned the needs of a plant, or a plant the needs of a man?

choices.text: Nothing, if the copying is done in the name of science
Nothing, because needs are conventional and kinds are not real
The nature that sets the needs has been ignored. One kind's requirement is not the other's
Nothing, if the person who copies the list is sincere

feedback.note: The assignment ignores the nature that sets the needs. A plant's requirements are not a man's, and a man's are not a plant's, because each follows from its own kind. Science does not consist in erasing identity, convention does not replace nature, and sincerity does not make a borrowed list true.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to the rule that the kind sets the needs.

pairs.right: What sets its needs
Needs that follow from a fish's life
Needs that follow from a man's life
Requirements copied from the wrong kind

feedback.note: The kind of organism sets its needs, so a fish's list follows from a fish's life and a man's from a man's. A borrowed list copies the wrong kind and therefore states requirements the borrower does not have, or drops requirements he does. Liking and decrees do not move an item from one nature to the other.

exercises.prompt: Every organism needs exactly what human beings need, because human needs are the ones that matter. What is the error?

choices.text: One kind is used as the template for every kind. Importance to us does not change another nature
The error is admitting that human beings have needs
The error is drawing any comparison between kinds
There is no error, because other natures are wishes we are free to edit

feedback.note: The error treats man's kind as the template for every kind. Importance to us does not change a fish's or a plant's nature. Admitting human needs is not the error, and comparison is how the difference is seen. Other natures are not wishes. Each kind sets its own requirements.

exercises.prompt: Does the rule that kind sets needs mean each member invents a private list?

choices.text: Yes. Needs are pure preferences, with one list invented per person
Yes. There is no nature for the members of a kind to share
No. Each person is his own species, so nothing can be shared
No. Members of a kind share its requirements. Circumstances change the means, not the source

feedback.note: Members of a kind share the requirements of that nature. A man in a desert and a man in a city both need water and the use of reason, while what they do to meet those needs can differ. Private invention fails because needs are not preferences, and a separate species for each person denies the kind they share.

exercises.prompt: Complete the principle that says where an organism's needs come from.

feedback.note: Needs follow from the kind of organism, because a requirement is a consequence of that nature. A wish, a vote, or a fashion fails because each can vary while the nature does not. Two kinds therefore do not share one list, and members of one kind do not each invent a private nature.

exercises.prompt: Build the principle that ties an organism's needs to its nature.

feedback.note: The kind of organism sets the needs of that organism, which is why a borrowed list fails. The wish would make the list a preference, and the vote would make it a convention. Circumstances can change how a need is met. They do not change which nature the need follows from, because the requirement is a fact of that kind.

exercises.prompt: Whose nature sets the needs of a human being?

choices.text: His own nature, the kind of living organism he is
A plant's nature, used because it is simpler to copy
A herd's nature, as if he lived by an automatic tribal code
Whatever he wishes the list to contain on a given day

feedback.note: Man's needs are set by man's nature, the kind of living organism he is. A plant's list and a herd's code fail because they are the wrong kinds, and a wish fails because it is not a nature. He is a rational animal, so the requirements of that integrated kind are his, not a simpler organism's and not a tribe's.

exercises.prompt: Why is graze and do not think not a human need?

choices.text: It is a need whenever it feels natural
It is not a requirement of man's life. His kind survives by reason, not by a grazer's pattern
It is a need because some other animals live that way
Thinking is a luxury added onto an animal code, and the code is the real need

feedback.note: Grazing without thought is not a requirement of man's life, because his kind survives by reason. Feeling natural fails because a mood is not his nature, another animal's pattern fails because the kind is different, and an animal code under a luxury of thought fails because he has no such code. Reason is not the extra.

exercises.prompt: A list of his needs is copied from whatever other people demand of him. Why does the list fail?

choices.text: It fails only if the people making the demands are few
It does not fail. His nature is whatever the demands say
Their demands are not his nature. His needs are requirements of his own life
A requirement of his life counts only after someone else has stated it

feedback.note: The list fails because other people's demands are not a reading of his nature. His needs are requirements of his own life as the organism he is. Numbers do not convert a demand into a nature, and a requirement does not wait to become real until someone else states it. A demand can be refused without erasing a real need.

exercises.prompt: Match each proposed source to its standing as an account of man's needs.

pairs.right: The source that sets his needs
The wrong kind to copy
Not a reading of his nature
The kind of organism he is

feedback.note: His own nature, that of a rational animal, sets his needs. Another species fails because it is the wrong kind to copy, and other people's demands fail because they are not a reading of his nature. The list includes what a rational living being requires, not what a plant requires and not what a crowd insists on.

exercises.prompt: Someone says man has no specific nature, so he has no needs, only poses. What has been denied?

choices.text: That he is a living organism of a definite kind, whose life has requirements
That people sometimes want things
That societies sometimes pass laws
That plants are alive

feedback.note: What has been denied is that man is a definite kind of living organism, so the requirements of that life are denied with it. Wants and laws are not the issue, because they can exist alongside real needs. The escape fails because he is something: a being with a specific nature, whose life therefore has requirements.

exercises.prompt: Man needs food, as an animal does, and the use of reason, as a plant does not. Which mistake drops one of those?

choices.text: Keeping both, on the ground that he is one organism
Comparing him with a plant at all
Saying that a hive's pattern is a third list he must also copy
Treating him as a mere body, or as a mere ghost, instead of as one rational animal

feedback.note: Dropping food treats him as a ghost, and dropping reason treats him as a mere body. His kind is one rational animal, so both belong to his needs. Keeping both is not the mistake. A comparison with a plant is how the difference shows, and a hive's pattern is another kind's list, not a third human requirement.

exercises.prompt: Complete the principle about the source of a human being's needs.

feedback.note: Man's needs follow from his nature, the nature of a rational animal, not from a whim, a herd, or a pose. A whim fails because preference is not requirement, a herd fails because he is not a tribal organism with an automatic code, and a pose fails because the denial of a nature does not remove the requirements of his life.

exercises.prompt: Build the principle that applies the rule about kinds to man.

feedback.note: Man's needs are the requirements of a rational animal, so both his physical requirements and the use of reason belong on the list. A plant would be the wrong kind, and a whim would replace nature with preference. Other people's demands do not rewrite the kind of organism he is, because a demand is not a nature.

exercises.prompt: Why does the use of reason belong among man's needs?

choices.text: He has no automatic code, and his life depends on identifying the facts
Reason is a pleasure one may add after survival is already secure
A group needs his agreement, and that social need creates the requirement
Instincts already secure his life, and reason only decorates them

feedback.note: The use of reason is a need because he has no automatic code and his life depends on identifying and integrating the facts. A later pleasure fails because the means is not an extra, a group's wish for agreement fails because the requirement is his nature, and instinct fails because he does not have that code.

exercises.prompt: Someone says he has food today, so thinking is optional. What has he missed?

choices.text: Nothing. Needs are only the physical items already in hand
Judging what he has, and dealing with what his life still requires, depend on reason
One stored meal changes his nature so that reason is no longer required
Reason runs as an instinct while he refuses to think

feedback.note: He has missed that the use of reason remains a need after one meal, because judging the food and meeting what comes next depend on it. Items already in hand are not the whole of his life's requirements. A meal does not change his nature, and reason does not run as an instinct while he blanks out.

exercises.prompt: Is the need for reason a need for true conclusions delivered without effort?

choices.text: Yes. Conclusions arrive on their own in a being of his kind
Yes. Error is impossible for a member of the rational kind
No. The need is to exercise the faculty. It does not hand him the knowledge
No, because reason is unrelated to any need he has

feedback.note: The need is to use reason, not to receive finished truths without effort. Conclusions do not arrive on their own, and error remains possible. Unrelatedness fails because his life depends on the faculty precisely in the absence of an automatic code. Possession of the faculty is not yet its use.

exercises.prompt: Match each description to the place of reason among man's needs.

pairs.right: A requirement of his life
What that use is not
What he does not have in reason's place
Does not retire the need to think

feedback.note: The use of reason is a requirement of his life, not an optional extra, because he has no automatic code in its place. One stored meal does not retire the need. The requirement is the exercise of the faculty, not a delivery of conclusions he never had to reach. Revelation does not retire it either.

exercises.prompt: A revelation is offered so that he can skip reason and still live as a man. Why does the need remain?

choices.text: A revelation is not a means of knowledge. His nature, not the offer, sets the need
The revelation is reason under a new name, so the need has been met
The need is only a custom, and he may vote it away
Skipping reason succeeds whenever the feeling that accompanies it is strong

feedback.note: The need remains because a revelation does not identify and integrate the facts, so it is not a means of knowledge, and his nature sets the requirement. Renaming the revelation as reason fails because the method was skipped. A vote cannot repeal a requirement of his kind, and a strong feeling is not evidence.

exercises.prompt: The need, someone says, is only to possess the faculty, whether or not it is used. What is wrong?

choices.text: Possession of the faculty is a fiction
Use is automatic once the faculty is possessed
Other people's thinking meets the need in his place
The need is to use reason. An unused faculty does not identify what his life depends on

feedback.note: The need is the use of reason, because an unused faculty does not identify the facts his life depends on. Possession is real, and it is not enough. Use is not automatic, which is why the need can be defaulted on. Other people's thinking does not focus his mind or meet the requirement for him.

exercises.prompt: Complete the principle that places reason among man's needs.

parts.text: The use of reason is a

feedback.note: The use of reason is a need of man's life, not a luxury, an ornament, or a whim. Those three name something he could skip without consequence, and he cannot, because he has no automatic code of knowledge or of values. The need is the exercise, not a stock of conclusions delivered in advance.

exercises.prompt: Build the principle that says why the use of reason is required.

feedback.note: Man needs to use reason because his life depends on it, given that no innate code supplies the knowledge and the values. May skip it would make the faculty optional, and as an ornament would place it after survival instead of inside the means of survival. One satisfied meal does not change the dependence.

exercises.prompt: Which statement holds the account of needs together?

choices.text: Needs follow from the kind of organism, and man's needs include the use of reason
Needs are wishes, reason is optional, and the kind of organism does not matter
A man's needs are whatever another species requires
Reason is his only need, because a ghost has no physical requirements

feedback.note: Needs follow from the kind of organism, and man's kind makes the use of reason one of his needs, together with the requirements of his life as an organism. Wishes fail because they are not requirements, another species is the wrong kind, and a ghost fails because he is not a mind detached from a body.

exercises.prompt: A need of his is unmet. What does that fact justify by itself?

choices.text: A right to seize what someone else has produced to meet the same need
The judgment that his life requires something he does not yet have, not a claim on another person's life or product
A duty in other people to serve the need, because the need is real
The conclusion that an unmet need was never more than a whim

feedback.note: An unmet need justifies the judgment that his life requires something he lacks. It does not, by itself, create a moral claim on another person's life or product. Seizure and a duty to serve treat the requirement as a mortgage. Calling it a whim denies the requirement in order to avoid the mortgage, which is a different error.

exercises.prompt: How are a man's needs properly met, once they are real?

choices.text: By seizing what others have produced, on the ground that the need is real
By an instinct that stocks the goods while he does not think
By thought and production, including an exchange the other person chooses
By declaring the need, which brings the missing goods into existence

feedback.note: Needs are met by thought and production, and by voluntary exchange when another person chooses to trade, because that is how a rational being acts on the requirements of his life. Seizure treats the need as a claim, instinct pretends to a code he does not have, and a declaration does not create the goods.

exercises.prompt: Match each part of the account of needs to the claim it makes.

pairs.right: Sets what the needs are
One of man's needs
How those requirements are met
What an unmet need does not create

feedback.note: The kind sets the needs, the use of reason is one of man's, thought and production are how they are met, and a right to seize is what an unmet need does not create. Collapsing the requirement into the claim fails because a fact about his life is not a title to someone else's product. Denying the fact is not required in order to deny the title.

exercises.prompt: You are hungry, and a neighbor has food. Your hunger is a real need. What follows?

choices.text: The need is a real requirement of your life, and it is not a mortgage on his food
His food is yours, because a real need transfers title
The hunger stops being a need if he declines to hand the food over
His ownership ends if you feel the hunger strongly enough

feedback.note: The hunger is a real need, a requirement of your life, and it is not a mortgage on his food. Title does not transfer with the need. His refusal does not turn the requirement into a whim, and the strength of the hunger does not rewrite ownership. Meeting the need is a matter of thought, production, or a trade he chooses.

exercises.prompt: If a need is not a claim on others, then it is not real. What has been collapsed?

choices.text: Two names for one fact, so the collapse is fair
A requirement and a whim, which were never different
Production and seizure, which meet a need in the same way
A fact about the organism and a moral claim on other people. Denying the claim leaves the requirement standing

feedback.note: A fact about what his life requires has been collapsed into a moral claim on other people. Denying the claim does not deny the requirement, and affirming the requirement does not create the claim. Production and seizure are not the same method. A whim was never the requirement at issue.

exercises.prompt: Complete the principle about how needs are met.

parts.text: Needs are met by thought and
, not by a right to seize.

feedback.note: Needs are met by thought and production, not by a right to seize, because a requirement of his life is not a title to another person's product. Seizure names the claim the principle rejects, instinct names a code he does not have, and a decree names the wish that the goods appear because the need was announced.

exercises.prompt: Build the principle that keeps a real need from becoming a right to take.

feedback.note: A need is a real requirement met by thought and production rather than seizure, because a fact about his life is not a title to someone else's product. A mere whim would deny that the requirement is real, and another's duty would turn it into a claim. His kind sets what is required. It does not set who else must supply it.

exercises.prompt: Can another person be a value to you, rather than a threat by existing?

choices.text: Yes. Knowledge, trade, friendship, and love can be values, and mere existence is not a threat
No. Other people are threats by the bare fact that they exist
No. A rational being gains nothing from dealing with other people
Yes, and therefore their purposes are automatically his duty

feedback.note: Another person can be a value, through knowledge, trade, friendship, or love, and his mere existence is not a threat. The lone-wolf denial fails because those gains are real. A threat by birth fails because existence is not an attack. Their purposes are not automatically his duty, which is a further claim the value does not include.

exercises.prompt: A person sells you a tool you could not make as well, on terms you both accept. What is he in that exchange?

choices.text: A member of a kind you are obliged to avoid
A value to you, through an exchange you both chose, not a threat and not an owner
A cell of one organism that includes both of you
A claim on you, created by the fact that he exists

feedback.note: He is a value through a chosen exchange, not a threat and not an owner. Avoidance fails because the tool is a real gain, a shared organism fails because two people are not one life, and a claim created by his existence fails because the value depended on terms both accepted. Mere coexistence did not produce the gain.

exercises.prompt: When is another person not a value to you?

choices.text: Whenever he is a separate person
Whenever he disagrees with a conclusion of yours
When he initiates force. Existing as a person does not by itself make him a value or a threat
Never. Every person is a value by being born

feedback.note: He is not a value when he initiates force, because the action attacks your life rather than offering a gain you can choose. Separate existence and disagreement are not attacks. Birth does not install a value, because what he does is what makes the difference. Existence alone is neither the value nor the threat.

exercises.prompt: Match each claim about other people to the fact or the error it names.

pairs.right: Knowledge, trade, friendship, or love
An error, because existence is not an attack
The lone denial of real human values
Ignores what the person actually does

feedback.note: Another person can be a value through knowledge, trade, friendship, or love. A threat by mere existence treats birth as an attack, the lone denial drops real gains, and value by birth ignores what he does. Force is what makes a person a threat, not the fact that he is a person. The gains still have to be judged.

exercises.prompt: Reason is an individual faculty, so a man needs nobody. What is mixed up in that inference?

choices.text: The faculty is his, and other people can still be values he judges and deals with
The mix-up is the claim that reason belongs to the individual
Other people think in his place, which is why the faculty is not his
Once he is rational, requirements of life no longer apply

feedback.note: Reason is an individual attribute, and that does not entail the lone conclusion that other people cannot be values. He judges and deals with them by his own faculty. Handing the thinking to them would deny the attribute. Requirements of life do not lapse. The values other people offer are among the goods a rational life can include.

exercises.prompt: Needing the values other people can offer is not a title to a particular person. Where is the line?

choices.text: A value counts only if he cannot last a day without that person
If he can last a day alone, then other people cannot be values
There is no line, because a value and a claim to seize someone are the same
The values are gained by chosen dealing. They are not a license to seize a life or a product

feedback.note: The line is between a value gained by chosen dealing and a license to seize. Needing what other people can offer does not entitle him to a particular person or product. Inability to last a day is not the test of a value, and the ability to last a day does not cancel the gains. Value and seizure are not the same fact.

exercises.prompt: Complete the principle about what another person can be.

feedback.note: Another person can be a value to you, through gains you judge and accept. Threat fails because mere existence is not an attack, master fails because a value is not an owner, and organ fails because he is not a part of a larger body. What he does, not the fact of birth, decides whether the gain is real.

exercises.prompt: Build the principle that says what mere existence does not settle.

feedback.note: Another person can be a value rather than a threat by merely existing, because existence is not an attack and the gains of trade, knowledge, and love are real. A master would turn the value into ownership, and an enemy by birth would restore the threat the principle rejects. Force, not birth, is what makes a person a threat.

exercises.prompt: What makes a relationship one in which another person can be a value?

choices.text: Both people choose it. He deals with others by voluntary agreement
One of them is not free to leave
The relationship was assigned before either person could consent
Living nearby creates it, whatever either person chooses

feedback.note: The relationship is a value when both people choose it, because he deals with others by voluntary agreement. A tie he cannot leave, an assignment before consent, and mere proximity fail because none of them is an agreement. Force does not become voluntary by being useful to the side that imposes it.

exercises.prompt: A builder and a client set terms both accept, and either may refuse. What kind of dealing is that?

choices.text: A bond the client was born owing to the builder
A voluntary agreement, in which each deals with the other by choice
The function of an organ inside one common organism
A duty created by the client's need, even if the builder refuses

feedback.note: It is a voluntary agreement, because each deals by choice and either may refuse. A bond by birth, an organ's function, and a duty created by need all drop the consent. The client's need may be real, and it does not obligate the builder. The value of the deal is the value each judged and accepted.

exercises.prompt: One side threatens the other into the exchange. Is this still a case of the other person as a chosen value?

choices.text: Yes, because both parties are human beings
Yes, because the result is useful to the side that made the threat
No. The threat removes agreement. A person under force has not chosen the tie
No, because every exchange, including one both accept, is a form of force

feedback.note: A threat removes the agreement, so the captive has not gained the other person as a chosen value. Being human is not consent, and usefulness to the aggressor is not a chosen gain for the victim. Calling every accepted exchange force fails because consent is exactly what distinguishes the agreement from the threat.

exercises.prompt: Match each relationship to the standing it has.

pairs.right: A voluntary agreement

pairs.left: A tie he is not free to leave
pairs.right: Not the dealing that makes the other a value

pairs.left: A refusal he is free to give
pairs.right: Part of dealing by agreement
Not an agreement

feedback.note: Terms both accept are a voluntary agreement, and the freedom to refuse is part of that dealing. A tie he cannot leave, and a role fixed before consent, are not agreements. Usefulness under threat does not repair the missing choice. He deals with others by agreement rather than by a bond that precedes any consent.

exercises.prompt: If he is free to refuse, someone says, the relationship cannot have value. What is wrong?

choices.text: The value includes the freedom to refuse. A tie he cannot leave is not made better by being inescapable
Nothing. Freedom to refuse shows that people are of no value to each other
An agreement is unreal whenever either person could have said no
Value requires that one side be unable to walk away

feedback.note: The value of the relationship depends on agreement, which includes the freedom to refuse. An inescapable tie is not made valuable by the fact that he cannot leave. Real agreements are chosen precisely because each person could have said no. Inability to walk away is force, not a deeper form of value.

exercises.prompt: Does a voluntary dealing mean that any whim, or any demand that the other submit, counts as an agreement?

choices.text: Yes. A standard would make the choice involuntary
Yes. Once both people speak, reason has nothing left to judge
No. Speech itself is force, even when both understand and accept the terms
No. An agreement is a chosen exchange each person judges. A demand that he submit is not one

feedback.note: Voluntary does not mean standardless. An agreement is a chosen exchange of values, judged by each person's reason. A whim that offers nothing, or a demand that the other submit, is not that exchange. Standards do not make choice involuntary. Accepted speech is not force. Force is what removes the choice.

exercises.prompt: Complete the principle about how a person deals with others.

parts.text: He deals with others by voluntary

feedback.note: He deals with others by voluntary agreement, not by ownership, instinct, or decree. Ownership would make one of them property, instinct would pretend to a tribal code, and a decree would replace consent. The agreement is judged by reason. It is not any set of words, and it is not a tie imposed before either person chooses, because consent is what makes the dealing voluntary.

exercises.prompt: Build the principle about the form of his dealing with other people.

feedback.note: He deals with other people by voluntary agreement, so the value of the relationship depends on choice on both sides. By force would remove the consent, and by birth would restore a tie that precedes any agreement. A need on one side does not turn the other person's refusal into a wrong.

exercises.prompt: Is society a living organism with a life of its own above the people in it?

choices.text: No. Society is a number of people. It has no mind and no life above theirs
Yes. The members are its cells, and its life is the one that counts
Yes, because people sometimes live near one another
No, because people are unable to be of any value to one another

feedback.note: Society is a number of individual people, not an organism with a mind and a life above theirs. Cells fail because persons are not organs of a super-organism. Nearness fails because proximity does not create a new living being. Denying that people can be values fails as the correction, because the values are real and the super-organism is not.

exercises.prompt: A number of people adopt an idea. Who did the thinking?

choices.text: The group, as a mind the members can only repeat
The individuals who judged it. A group has no mind that thought in their place
Society, an organism whose idea the members find already inside themselves
An instinct shared at birth, of which the idea is a copy

feedback.note: The individuals who judged the idea did the thinking, because a group has no consciousness. A group mind and a social organism both invent a thinker that is not there. An instinct fails because the idea was judged, not copied from a code. Agreement among people is a set of judgments, not a new mind.

exercises.prompt: A speaker says society wants something no person has judged, and treats that want as a natural fact. What has he invented?

choices.text: A voluntary agreement among the people who in fact want it
The ordinary fact that one person can be a value to another
A super-organism with purposes of its own. Only people have purposes
A reminder that people are able to communicate a judgment

feedback.note: He has invented a super-organism with purposes of its own. Only people have purposes, so a want that no person judged is not a fact of nature. An agreement would require people who had judged it. Communication is real, and it fails as a group mind because talkers are not a mind above the communicators.

exercises.prompt: Match each picture of a group to the claim it makes.

pairs.right: What a society consists of
A life alleged to stand above the members
A thinker that does not exist
His own, not the function of an organ

feedback.note: Society consists of individual people. A super-organism and a group mind fail because they add a life and a thinker that are not there. A person's purpose is his own, not an organ's function in a larger body. Rules and budgets of an association remain tools of people. They do not hatch a new organism.

exercises.prompt: Does rejecting a social organism mean that people are unrelated atoms?

choices.text: No. They can deal, trade, and care for one another. What fails is a life that owns them as organs
Yes. Without a social organism, no relationship is real
Yes. Values between people would require a group mind
No, because the rejection was a mistake and society is an animal

feedback.note: People can deal, trade, and care for one another without being organs of a further animal. Unrelated atoms are the wrong correction. Values between them do not require a group mind, because each person judges the value. Society is not an animal whose life outranks theirs. The relationships are real, and they are relationships of individuals.

exercises.prompt: An association has rules and a budget. Does that make the association an organism?

choices.text: Yes. To be organized is the same fact as to be an organism
Yes. A budget is a purpose the association feels as a body
No. Associations are impossible unless they are organisms
No. Rules and a budget are agreements and tools of people, not a mind above them

feedback.note: Rules and a budget are agreements and tools of people, so the association is not an organism and does not feel purposes. Organization is not the same fact as a living body. The association can exist as a chosen arrangement precisely because it is not a new animal. A mind above the members is what the tools do not create.

exercises.prompt: Complete the principle that rejects a super-organism.

feedback.note: Society is not a living organism above its members, because only the members are alive and conscious. Agreement, a market, and friendship fail in the blank because those are relationships of people, not a further living body. The relationships can be valuable. They do not add a mind that thinks for the people in them.

exercises.prompt: Build the principle that says what a society is not.

feedback.note: Society is not an organism with a life above its members. A marketplace and an agreement are dealings among people, which is a different claim and not the error being rejected. The error is the super-organism that thinks and wants, because only people judge, agree, and pursue purposes.

exercises.prompt: Does society own the individual who lives among other people?

choices.text: No. He is not the property of other people, of a majority, or of an institution
Yes, because he lives among them
Yes, because he can gain values from them
Yes, in the way an organ belongs to the animal that contains it

feedback.note: Society does not own the individual. He is not the property of other people, a majority, or an institution. Living among them and gaining values from them do not transfer title. The organ comparison fails because society is not an animal and he is not a part. Ownership of his life remains his.

exercises.prompt: A rule treats a person's work as the public's because he lives in the country. What is being claimed?

choices.text: That he may trade with people who choose to trade with him
That society owns him and the product of his effort. Residence is not a title
That reason is an attribute of the person who works
That a need is a requirement of the worker's life

feedback.note: The rule claims that society owns him and the product of his effort, and residence is not a title. Trade, the attribute of reason, and the reality of needs are different propositions. None of them says that living in a place assigns his work to the public, because a benefit he has received is not a purchase of the person.

exercises.prompt: If society does not own a person's life, whose life is it?

choices.text: The majority's, held until he dissents
Nobody's, because a life cannot belong to the being who lives it
His. Other people may deal with him, and they hold no title to him
The state's, under a name gentler than property

feedback.note: The life is his. Other people may deal with him by agreement, and they hold no title. A majority's custody until dissent is still a claim of ownership. Nobody's life fails because he is the being whose life it is. A gentler name for the state's title is the same claim of ownership.

exercises.prompt: Match each item to the ownership claim that fits it.

pairs.right: Not the property of society
Holder of no title to his life or his work
The picture of membership to reject
Not a transfer of title

feedback.note: The individual is not society's property, and society holds no title to his life or his work. An organ of a body is the picture to reject, because he is not a part of a larger animal. Living among others is not a transfer of title. Gratitude and trade are compatible with that fact, and neither one sells him.

exercises.prompt: He has benefited from roads others built, so his life belongs to the public. What is the error?

choices.text: A benefit is not a purchase of the person. Past goods are not a title to his life
The error is using a road
Benefits are impossible if a person is not property
The public is a biological organism, so the title is a fact of nature

feedback.note: A benefit is not a purchase of the person. Goods others produced, even goods he has used, are not a title to his life, because use is not a deed. Refusing the road is not required. Benefits are possible among people who own their own lives, by payment and agreement. The public is not a biological organism that could hold a natural title.

exercises.prompt: Rejecting social ownership still leaves gratitude and trade. What is the line?

choices.text: Gratitude confesses that he is owned
Trade transfers title to his life
An agreement assigns him to the other party as property
He can pay for values and keep agreements. None of that makes him anyone's property

feedback.note: He can pay for values, keep agreements, and regard other people as values, and none of that makes him property. Gratitude is not a confession of title, trade does not sell the trader, and an agreement does not assign the person. The line is between a chosen dealing and a claim that society owns him.

exercises.prompt: Complete the principle that residence confers no title.

feedback.note: Living among others does not transfer ownership of one's life, because company is not a deed. Knowledge, friendship, and speech fail in the blank because those can be shared without becoming title to the person. A road he uses and a law he lives under are not purchases of him either.

exercises.prompt: Build the principle that company confers no title.

feedback.note: Living among others does not make a person their property. Customer and neighbor name relationships he can actually have, and they are not titles to his life. The error is ownership, including ownership described as an organ's place in a social body. His work remains his unless he chooses to trade it.

exercises.prompt: Which pair is the full account of a person living among other people?

choices.text: Others can be a value by voluntary agreement, and society neither thinks nor owns him
Others are threats, and society must own him if he is to be safe
He gains nothing from others, and agreement is a form of weakness
Society is the organism, and its purposes are a duty he is born into

feedback.note: Others can be a value in a voluntary agreement, and society is not an organism that owns him or a mind whose purposes he must serve. Threat plus ownership fails because it is the tribal picture. Gaining nothing fails because it is the lone picture. A duty by birth collapses company into a claim on his life. The two truths stand together.

exercises.prompt: Why does living with other people not make their purposes his duty?

choices.text: Because other people are incapable of being values
Their purposes are theirs. He joins them when he judges the dealing a value, not because company is a mortgage
Because duty is an instinct, and instinct is what he should follow instead
Because a group mind's purposes outrank his judgment, so the question cannot arise

feedback.note: Their purposes remain theirs. He deals with them when he judges the dealing a value, and living with them is not a mortgage on his life. Incapacity for value is the wrong reason, because the values are real. Instinct is not a code he has, and a group mind does not outrank a judgment he has to make for himself.

exercises.prompt: What stands between the lone refusal of other people and the tribal claim that the group comes first?

choices.text: He is a cell of the group, and his agreement is irrelevant
He needs no one, and a gain from another person confesses failure
He needs the values other people can offer, and he deals with them by voluntary agreement
He deals with them by force, because a need cancels the other person's consent

feedback.note: He needs the values other people can offer, and he deals with them by voluntary agreement. That is neither the lone refusal nor the tribal claim that the group comes first. A cell has no agreement to make, a confession of failure denies the values, and force pretends that a need cancels consent. Consent is the form of the dealing.

exercises.prompt: Match each idea to the place it has among men.

pairs.right: Can be a value when both choose the relationship
Not an organism and not an owner
Not his duty merely because he lives with them
Denies the values other people can offer

feedback.note: Another person can be a value in a relationship both choose, society is neither an organism nor an owner, and other people's purposes are not his duty merely because he lives with them. The lone refusal denies real values. Holding the value does not create the duty, and rejecting the duty does not erase the value.

exercises.prompt: A city offers trade, friendship, and a law against force. A speaker adds that the city therefore owns the citizens and that its plan is their duty. What do you keep?

choices.text: The voluntary values. Drop ownership, and drop the plan as a duty
The ownership, and drop the trade, because title is the real value
Nothing. A city is either a super-organism or it is nothing at all
The plan, because a group mind knows the citizens' good in their place

feedback.note: Keep the values of voluntary life with others, and drop both the ownership and the duty to the plan. Title is not the value. A city can be a network of agreements without being a super-organism. A group mind does not know their good in their place, because only the citizens judge. Company created no mortgage.

exercises.prompt: If their purposes are not his duty, then he may never help anyone. What has been slid together?

choices.text: Help and force, treated as the same action
A duty and a whim, so that helping is a form of knowledge
Their purposes and his, which a group mind makes identical
A duty imposed by their purposes, and help he chooses because he values it. No duty is not a ban on chosen help

feedback.note: A duty imposed by their purposes has been slid together with help he chooses because he judges it a value. The absence of a duty is not a ban on help. Help is not force, a whim is not knowledge, and a group mind does not make their purposes his. He can value another person and still refuse to be owned or conscripted.

exercises.prompt: Complete the principle about purposes that are not his.

parts.text: He deals with their purposes by agreement and judgment, not by

feedback.note: He deals with their purposes by agreement and judgment, not by duty, because company does not mortgage him to ends he has not chosen. Reason, trade, and choice fail in the blank because those are how he deals, not the imposition being rejected. Chosen help remains possible. What is rejected is a purpose of theirs becoming his assignment.

exercises.prompt: Build the principle that joins the need of other people with the form of the dealing.

feedback.note: He needs other people and deals with them by voluntary agreement, so the gains are real and the form is consent. As their property would make society the owner, and by tribal duty would make their purposes his assignment. Neither follows from the need, because a group remains a number of people, not a life that thinks or owns its members.
